knownFor: Convert and writer of Carthage, the foremost early writer of the faith in Latin. In the Apology he defended the Christians before Rome's governors; in the Prescription he claimed the Scriptures for the churches the apostles founded; in Against Praxeas he put the Latin words trinitas, persona and substantia to work for God as one substance in three persons. He later took up the strict New Prophecy, and Augustine counted his followers, the Tertullianists, among the heretics.
datesNote: No source gives his birth or his death. Jerome says only that he flourished chiefly under the emperors Severus and Antoninus Caracalla and is said to have lived to a decrepit old age. The note to the English Eusebius gives the common view of a birth about 160, and Nöldechen's conclusion of a birth about 150 and a death about 230; the note to the English Jerome gives a birth about 160 and a death about 245. Monceaux dates the Apology to 197, the Prescription to about 200, the turn to the New Prophecy to 207 to 212, the final break with the church to the start of 213, Against Praxeas to after 213, and On Modesty to between 217 and 222, probably the last of his surviving books. McGiffert says almost all scholars place the Apology in 197 to 204 and holds 197 practically established; older views give 198 (Mosheim) and 204 (Kaye)
placeNote: Carthage, in the Roman province of Africa, today in Tunisia (Jerome: of the city of Carthage in the province of Africa); Eusebius calls him one of those especially distinguished in Rome
role: Writer in Latin at Carthage; convert, versed in Roman law by Eusebius's account; later a follower of the New Prophecy

keyWorks.title: Apology
keyWorks.about: a defense of the Christians addressed to the governors who sat as judges for Rome: the charge is only the name, the crowd blames the Christians for every flood, drought, famine and plague, and the more they are cut down, the more they grow

keyWorks.title: The Prescription Against Heretics
keyWorks.about: a plea of the kind the law courts call a demurrer, a formal objection that throws a case out before it is argued: those who teach against the apostles may not argue from Scripture at all, because the Scriptures belong to the churches that received them from the apostles, such as Ephesus and Rome

keyWorks.title: Against Praxeas
keyWorks.about: written after his turn to the New Prophecy, against a teacher at Rome who, by Tertullian's account, said the Father himself was born and suffered; he answers that God is one substance and three persons, distinct but not divided, and the Latin words trinitas, persona and substantia stand in his text

traces: Jerome heard, through two people, that Cyprian never let a day pass without reading him and would say to his secretary, Give me the master. Benson calls Cyprian his devoted yet discriminating disciple and prints a table of Cyprian's verbal debts to him in the treatise on the Lord's Prayer.
Jerome says Novatian's book On the Trinity is a sort of epitome of the work of Tertullian; Harnack finds that not borne out.

The Latin words he put to work in Against Praxeas, trinitas, persona and substantia, became the Latin church's words for God, as the census and later editors say; Sanday credits him with coining terms and marking out the main lines of Latin theology.

Augustine says his followers, the Tertullianists, dwindled to a last remnant at Carthage; the very few left crossed to the Catholic church and handed over their basilica, which he calls still well known.
remembered: Lactantius says he was skilled in literature of every kind but had little readiness in eloquence, was not polished and was very obscure, so that he did not find sufficient renown; elsewhere Lactantius says he fully pleaded the same cause in the treatise entitled the Apology.
Augustine says many of his little works, most eloquently written, are read.

Vincent of Lérins, in 434, gives him by far the first place among the Latins, as Origen has among the Greeks, then calls him more eloquent than faithful, quotes Hilary that by his subsequent error he detracted from the authority of his approved writings, and says he was a great trial in the Church.
Jerome calls him a man of keen and vigorous character.

uncertain: Nearly all that is known of his life comes from his own books and from Jerome's short life of him, written about 170 years later. Eusebius and Lactantius wrote about a century after him, and Augustine and Vincent about two centuries. No source says when or why he was converted; McGiffert's guess of between 180 and 190 is an editor's.

Trained in the law. Eusebius calls him a man well versed in the laws of the Romans, but his translator's note says this knowledge is not very conspicuous in his writings. McGiffert says he became a lawyer and rhetorician in Rome and very likely practiced; Sanday calls him primarily a lawyer. Monceaux holds his legal training and his fondness for the language of the courts beyond question, but says that identifying him with the jurist Tertullian quoted in the Digest is only a hypothesis, that the name was common, and that the jurist may be a relative. Whether he practiced as an advocate is not settled.

Why he turned to the New Prophecy. Jerome says he was driven to the doctrine of Montanus by the envy and abuse of the clergy of the Roman church. Augustine says he went over to the Phrygians whom he had earlier refuted, began to condemn second marriage as fornication against the apostle's teaching, and later broke from them too and spread his own gatherings.

From whom he withdrew. He says his side withdrew from the carnally-minded on its acknowledgment of the Paraclete. The editor Coxe reads this as perhaps only a withdrawal from the communion of the bishop of Rome, not a final break with his own bishop and the church of North Africa; Monceaux reads a break with the church at Carthage and dates it to the start of 213; Augustine says he later broke from the New Prophecy too.

His office. That he was a presbyter rests only on Jerome, who says he was one until middle life; Monceaux accepts it and thinks he was ordained about 200, since he speaks as a simple believer in the Apology of 197; McGiffert's note says it cannot be told whether he served at Rome or at Carthage.

First in Latin. Jerome places him first among the Latin writers after Victor and Apollonius, and the census calls him the first major Christian author to write in Latin. Coxe calls him the founder of Latin Christianity and dates the Octavius of Minucius Felix to about 210, as his contemporary; Wallis, in the same volume, says the Octavius's date is keenly disputed and may be about 166, which would make it older.

The Latin words. The census says he invented trinitas, persona, substantia and sacramentum; the held sources show the first three in his text, and Sanday credits him with coining terms. Coxe notes that Theophilus of Antioch used the Greek word for a triad, the earliest use of the word Trinity he knows, so the Greek word is older. Kaye thought the Athanasian Creed was composed by one who had Against Praxeas always in mind; that is an editor's view. No held source says the Council of Nicaea used his words.

Praxeas and the bishop's edict. What is known of Praxeas comes from Tertullian's own hostile account. The English edition's editor says the bishop of Rome who withdrew his letter of peace was probably Victor; Monceaux says the edict that On Modesty answers was Callistus's, and which bishop issued it is disputed.

What is probably his last surviving book. Monceaux dates On Modesty to 217 to 222 and calls it very probably the last of the surviving works; Jerome says many of his small works are not extant, and Eusebius's translator says a few of his works were written in Greek.

Cyprian's words. The report that Cyprian read him daily and said, Give me the master, reaches us through Jerome, from the old man Paul of Concordia, who had met Cyprian's aged secretary at Rome. Jerome's Latin says so; the English translation of Jerome wrongly makes Paul himself the secretary, while Heurtley, quoting Kaye, reads it as the Latin does and gives the words as Give me my master.

Novatian. Jerome calls Novatian's On the Trinity a sort of epitome of Tertullian's work, and says many mistakenly ascribe it to Cyprian; Harnack says the claim that it epitomizes a work of Tertullian, which can only be Against Praxeas, is not borne out.

His father. Jerome's Latin says patre centurione proconsulari, a centurion on the governor's staff, and his Chronicle says the same; the English translation of the Lives reads son of a proconsul or Centurion, which is a mistranslation, and Heurtley's quotation of Kaye reads the son of a proconsular centurion.

Vincent's verdict. The English reads more eloquent by far than faithful, but its editor notes that Baluze reads fidelior and others read felicior, so the reading is disputed. Hilary's judgment reaches us here only through Vincent in English. The decree wrongly called Gelasian lists Opuscula Tertulliani among the books not received, beside the History of Eusebius and the works of Lactantius; Mansi puts it at about 496 and says its author has long been disputed.
The Passion of Perpetua and Felicitas. It was handed down with his works; Coxe thinks Tertullian was the editor of the story, not its author, which is an editor's guess.

The quoted Latin. The Latin of the Apology and the Prescription is held only in Oehler's 1853 edition in a damaged scan, which has lost words and garbled others; no other held print confirms them, so these quotations are printed in English alone, except two short lines the scan prints cleanly, the blood of Christians is seed and I am the heir of the apostles, which carry the Latin. For Against Praxeas the two held Latin prints differ: Kroymann reads ubique teneo with etsi added in brackets, and Oehler reads ubique teneam with no etsi.

briefReferences: Apology 1 (Thelwall): the hidden road of silent writing and the plea not to be condemned unknown, from the first chapter; the brief puts the book at about 197, as Monceaux does.

Church History II.2 (McGiffert's translation): Eusebius calls him well versed in the laws of the Romans. Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 53: Carthage. Vincent of Lérins, Commonitory 18: the first place among the Latins.
Augustine, On Heresies 86: the Tertullianists, and Tertullian named a heretic for going over to the Phrygians.
Apology 40 and 50 (Thelwall): the crowd blames the Christians for flood, drought, famine and plague, and the close, the more we are mown down the more we grow, the blood of Christians is seed.

Prescription Against Heretics 15, 19, 21, 36 and 37 (Holmes): whose the Scriptures are, the faith handed from Christ to the apostles and their churches such as Ephesus and Rome, and the property lines about timber, springs and heirs.

Against Praxeas 1 (Holmes): his side separated from the carnally-minded by the Paraclete, who in the brief is the Holy Spirit; On Monogamy 1 and On Fasting: the stricter rules of the New Prophecy; Monceaux on Flight in Persecution: no flight from persecution. Jerome, Lives 53, and Augustine, On Heresies 86: the two reasons given for the turn.

Against Praxeas 1, 2 and 12 (Holmes; Latin in Kroymann and Oehler): Praxeas and the Father who was born and suffered by Tertullian's account, the word another as person and not substance, and one substance in three who are joined together; the words trinitas, persona and substantia.

On Modesty (Thelwall; Latin in CSEL 20): the bishop's offer to forgive adultery after repentance, and the church of the Spirit against a church that is a number of bishops; Monceaux on its date and place among his surviving books.
Jerome, Lives 70, on Novatian's book, with Harnack's doubt; Jerome, Lives 53, the report of Cyprian and the master; Lactantius, Divine Institutes V.4, on the Apology.

Augustine, On Heresies 86: the last of the Tertullianists handed their basilica to the Catholic church. Jerome, Lives 53: said to have lived to a decrepit old age; Eusebius's translator on the main sources of his life.
World census, The Case Made in Latin: his tradition.

quotationOriginals.modern: Then let the truth reach your ears at least by the hidden road of silent writing.
quotationOriginals.printed: you cannot surely forbid the Truth to reach your ears by the secret pathway of a noiseless book.
quotationOriginals.work: Apology 1, tr. S. Thelwall, in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 3
quotationOriginals.uncertain: The Latin is held only in a damaged scan, so the English stands alone. The modern wording follows the Latin: silent writing is tacitarum litterarum, where Thelwall has a noiseless book.

quotationOriginals.modern: One thing only she asks for now: not to be condemned unknown.
quotationOriginals.printed: One thing, meanwhile, she anxiously desires of earthly rulers—not to be condemned unknown.
quotationOriginals.work: Apology 1, tr. S. Thelwall, in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 3
quotationOriginals.uncertain: The Latin is held only in a damaged scan, so the English stands alone. This sentence comes in chapter 1; the Apology goes on after it and closes in chapter 50.

quotationOriginals.modern: the blood of Christians is seed.
quotationOriginals.printed: the blood of Christians is seed
quotationOriginals.work: Apology 50, tr. S. Thelwall, in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 3
quotationOriginals.uncertain: The popular form, the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church, is not his wording.

quotationOriginals.modern: By what right, Marcion, do you cut my timber? By whose leave, Valentinus, do you turn my springs aside?
quotationOriginals.printed: Indeed, Marcion, by what right do you hew my wood? By whose permission, Valentinus, are you diverting the streams of my fountain?
quotationOriginals.work: The Prescription Against Heretics 37, tr. Holmes, in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 3
quotationOriginals.uncertain: The Latin is held only in a damaged scan that has lost words and garbled others, so the English stands alone. Cut before this: Who are you? When and whence did you come? As you are none of mine, what have you to do with that which is mine? Cut after it: By what power, Apelles, are you removing my landmarks? This is my property. Why are you, the rest, sowing and feeding here at your own pleasure?

quotationOriginals.modern: This property is mine. I have held it long; I held it first.
quotationOriginals.printed: This (I say) is my property. I have long possessed it; I possessed it before you.
quotationOriginals.work: The Prescription Against Heretics 37, tr. Holmes, in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 3
quotationOriginals.uncertain: The Latin is held only in a damaged scan, so the English stands alone. This is the second time the sentence This is my property comes in the passage; the cut before it is given on the span above. Cut after it: I hold sure title-deeds from the original owners themselves, to whom the estate belonged.

quotationOriginals.modern: I am the heir of the apostles.
quotationOriginals.printed: I am the heir of the apostles.
quotationOriginals.work: The Prescription Against Heretics 37, tr. Holmes, in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 3

quotationOriginals.modern: I have already said how you should take the word 'another'. It names a person, not a substance. It marks a distinction, not a division. I hold everywhere one substance in three who are joined together.
quotationOriginals.printed: In what sense, however, you ought to understand Him to be another, I have already explained, on the ground of Personality, not of Substance—in the way of distinction, not of division. But although I must everywhere hold one only substance in three coherent and inseparable (Persons)
quotationOriginals.work: Against Praxeas 12, tr. Holmes, in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 3
quotationOriginals.original: alium autem quomodo accipere debeas, iam professus sum, personae, non substantiae nomine, ad distinctionem, non ad diuisionem. ceterum, (etsi) ubique teneo unam substantiam in tribus cohaerentibus
quotationOriginals.uncertain: Holmes's (Persons) and inseparable are his own additions; the Latin has only in three who cohere. The Latin is held in two prints that differ: Kroymann reads ubique teneo with etsi added in brackets, and Oehler reads ubique teneam with no etsi; the modern wording and the Latin given here follow Kroymann. Kroymann's scan misreads distinctionem, which Oehler's print confirms. The brief stops after the fourth sentence; the next, Yet the sense forces me to call the one who commands another than the one who makes, is cut.
